content: Superphosphate is a type of fertilizer that is produced through the chemical reaction of concentrated sulfuric acid with powdered phosphate rock. In the 1840s, scientists discovered that coprolites, which are fossilized animal feces, could be dissolved in sulfuric acid to create what became known as superphosphate. In 1840, Justus von Liebig wrote, The crops on the field diminish or increase in exact proportion to the diminution or increase of the mineral substances conveyed to it in manure. Von Liebig was the first to identify that the phosphate of lime found in bone meal could be made more accessible to plants by treating it with sulfuric acid. Around the same time, Sir John Bennet Lawes discovered that phosphate rock underwent a similar reaction when treated with sulfuric acid and could serve as a source material for producing superphosphate. Bennet Lawes was the first to manufacture superphosphate on an industrial scale at his factory in Deptford, England, in 1842. The demand for superphosphate grew significantly in the second half of the 20th century, particularly due to the development of aerial topdressing in New Zealand. This innovation allowed superphosphate to be economically distributed over large areas of farmland. Superphosphate can also form naturally in large quantities through the action of guano, or bird feces, which leads to deposits around seabird colonies. These deposits can be mined for use as fertilizer. One of the most well-known sites for mining such deposits is the island of Nauru in the South Pacific. The mining of phosphate-rich soil on Nauru brought temporary wealth to its inhabitants but caused severe environmental destruction.
